title: 2 Kings 9:14–29
context: Jehu conspires against King Joram, who is recovering in Jezreel from wounds received fighting Hazael of Syria (8:28–29), and who is being visited by Ahaziah king of Judah. Jehu drives to Jezreel; messengers sent to ask whether he comes in peace join his company instead. Joram and Ahaziah ride out and meet him on the land of Naboth the Jezreelite. Jehu kills Joram with an arrow and has his body thrown onto Naboth’s field, citing the LORD’s word against Ahab for Naboth’s blood (1 Kings 21:19, 29). Ahaziah flees and is mortally wounded, dying at Megiddo, and is buried in Jerusalem. 8:25 dates Ahaziah’s accession to Joram’s twelfth year, while 9:29 says the eleventh; interpreters account for the difference in more than one way. The narrator presents these events as the beginning of the judgment Elijah announced.

verses.text: So Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi conspired against Joram. (Now Joram was defending Ramoth Gilead, he and all Israel, because of Hazael king of Syria;
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu conspires against Joram, who had been defending Ramoth Gilead against Hazael. Arminian readers note that the narrator plainly calls it a conspiracy, reporting the human politics behind the events.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s purposes working through a political coup without the narrator approving every act within it. Both traditions read the verse as joining prophetic commission and human scheming in a single course of events.

verses.text: but King Joram had returned to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds which the Syrians had given him when he fought with Hazael king of Syria.) Jehu said, “If this is your thinking, then let no one escape and go out of the city to go to tell it in Jezreel.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joram has gone to Jezreel to heal from wounds received from the Syrians, and Jehu orders that no one leave to warn him. Arminian readers note Jehu’s careful planning to keep the coup secret.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the circumstances, including Joram’s wounds, as part of God’s providence arranging the moment of judgment. Shared ground: the verse recalls 8:28–29 and explains why both kings are in Jezreel.

verses.text: So Jehu rode in a chariot and went to Jezreel, for Joram lay there. Ahaziah king of Judah had come down to see Joram.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu rides to Jezreel, where Joram lies and Ahaziah king of Judah has come to visit. Arminian readers note that Ahaziah’s presence is unplanned from his point of view, placing him in the path of the coup.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the meeting of the two kings in Jezreel as providentially arranged. Both traditions note that Ahaziah was related to Ahab through his mother (8:26–27), which helps explain why he is drawn into what follows.

verses.text: Now the watchman was standing on the tower in Jezreel, and he spied the company of Jehu as he came, and said, “I see a company.” Joram said, “Take a horseman, and send to meet them, and let him say, ‘Is it peace?’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The watchman on the tower in Jezreel sees Jehu’s company, and Joram sends a horseman to ask, “Is it peace?” Arminian readers note the repeated question, which runs through the whole chapter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the question of peace as ironic, since there can be no peace for Ahab’s house under judgment. Shared ground: the repeated question frames the narrative, preparing for Jehu’s answer in 9:22.

verses.text: So one went on horseback to meet him, and said, “the king says, ‘Is it peace?’ ” Jehu said, “What do you have to do with peace? Fall in behind me!” The watchman said, “The messenger came to them, but he isn’t coming back.”
verses.arminianNotes: The messenger asks about peace, and Jehu tells him to fall in behind; the watchman reports that he does not return. Arminian readers note that the messenger chooses to join Jehu rather than return to the king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the defections a sign that Joram’s support is collapsing. Both traditions read the verse as building tension, with each messenger who goes out failing to return to the king.

verses.text: Then he sent out a second on horseback, who came to them and said, “The king says, ‘Is it peace?’ ” Jehu answered, “What do you have to do with peace? Fall in behind me!”
verses.arminianNotes: A second horseman comes with the same question and receives the same answer. Arminian readers note the repetition, which shows Jehu’s control of the situation and the growing isolation of the king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the pattern as emphasizing that events are moving steadily toward the outcome announced by the prophet. Shared ground: the repeated scene is a narrative device that slows the story before the confrontation.

verses.text: The watchman said, “He came to them, and isn’t coming back. The driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi, for he drives furiously.”
verses.arminianNotes: The watchman recognizes Jehu by his furious driving. Arminian readers note the vivid detail, which gives a sense of Jehu’s personality as forceful and determined.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the description as fitting a man appointed for swift judgment, without implying approval of his temperament. Both traditions read the detail as characterization, not as a moral comment on Jehu.

verses.text: Joram said, “Get ready!” They got his chariot ready. Then Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah went out, each in his chariot; and they went out to meet Jehu, and found him on Naboth the Jezreelite’s land.
verses.arminianNotes: Joram and Ahaziah ride out and meet Jehu on Naboth the Jezreelite’s land. Arminian readers note the significance of the location, where Ahab and Jezebel had taken Naboth’s vineyard by murder (1 Kings 21).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the meeting place as God’s justice returning to the scene of the crime. Shared ground: the narrator deliberately names Naboth’s land, inviting readers to connect what follows with Elijah’s word against Ahab.

verses.text: When Joram saw Jehu, he said, “Is it peace, Jehu?” He answered, “What peace, so long as the prostitution of your mother Jezebel and her witchcraft abound?”
verses.arminianNotes: Joram asks if it is peace, and Jehu answers that there can be no peace while Jezebel’s prostitution and witchcraft abound. Arminian readers note that the language is often read as describing idolatry rather than literal acts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Jehu naming the idolatry fostered by Jezebel as the root of Israel’s trouble. Both traditions read the answer as tying the coup to the religious corruption of Ahab’s house, while hedging how literally the terms are meant.

verses.text: Joram turned his hands and fled, and said to Ahaziah, “This is treason, Ahaziah!”
verses.arminianNotes: Joram turns and flees, crying treason to Ahaziah. Arminian readers note that Joram recognizes the danger immediately, and his cry shows that he understands the meeting as a rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king’s flight as the moment when the judgment on Ahab’s house begins to fall. Shared ground: the verse reports the turning point plainly, without comment on the rights of either side.

verses.text: Jehu drew his bow with his full strength, and struck Joram between his arms; and the arrow went out at his heart, and he sunk down in his chariot.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu shoots Joram with his bow, and the king falls in his chariot. Arminian readers state the event as the text gives it, noting that Joram dies as the son of Ahab under the sentence pronounced on his father’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the death as part of the judgment announced earlier, while recognizing that the text does not invite celebration. Both traditions report the killing soberly, as the narrative does.

verses.text: Then Jehu said to Bidkar his captain, “Pick him up, and throw him in the plot of the field of Naboth the Jezreelite; for remember how, when you and I rode together after Ahab his father, the LORD laid this burden on him:
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu orders Joram’s body thrown into Naboth’s field, recalling the burden the LORD laid on Ahab. Arminian readers note that Jehu presents himself as a witness to the earlier prophecy, linking his act to it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the placement of the body as fulfilling the word of the LORD against Ahab’s house. Shared ground: the verse connects Joram’s death with the injustice done to Naboth, which the narrative has not forgotten.

verses.text: ‘Surely I have seen yesterday the blood of Naboth, and the blood of his sons,’ says the LORD; ‘and I will repay you in this plot of ground,’ says the LORD. Now therefore take and cast him onto the plot of ground, according to the LORD’s word.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu recalls the LORD’s word about the blood of Naboth and his sons. Arminian readers note that this verse adds the detail of Naboth’s sons, not mentioned in 1 Kings 21, and that judgment was delayed to Ahab’s son (1 Kings 21:29).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s justice for the innocent as certain, even when carried out a generation later. Both traditions read the verse as the narrator’s explicit link between Joram’s death and the LORD’s word concerning Naboth.

verses.text: But when Ahaziah the king of Judah saw this, he fled by the way of the garden house. Jehu followed after him, and said, “Strike him also in the chariot!” They struck him at the ascent of Gur, which is by Ibleam. He fled to Megiddo, and died there.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaziah flees, is struck near Ibleam at the ascent of Gur, and dies at Megiddo. Arminian readers note that the locations are given precisely, though the site of Gur is uncertain and Ibleam’s identification is debated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Chronicles 22:9 gives a different account of where Ahaziah was found, and the two are harmonized in various ways. Shared ground: Ahaziah’s death is reported briefly, as part of the downfall of Ahab’s extended house.

verses.text: His servants carried him in a chariot to Jerusalem, and buried him in his tomb with his fathers in David’s city.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaziah’s servants carry him to Jerusalem and bury him in David’s city. Arminian readers note that, unlike Joram, he receives an honorable burial among the kings of Judah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the burial in David’s city as a reminder that the Davidic line continues despite this king’s ties to Ahab. Both traditions read the verse as a quiet ending for a king caught up in judgment on his mother’s family.

verses.text: In the eleventh year of Joram the son of Ahab, Ahaziah began to reign over Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaziah began to reign in Joram’s eleventh year. Arminian readers note that 8:25 gives the twelfth year; the two notices differ, and interpreters account for the difference in more than one way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same difference and avoid resolving it with more certainty than the text allows. Shared ground: the verse is a regnal notice placed at the end of Ahaziah’s story, not a statement about the events just described.
